name: Medium Carmine
lede: Medium Carmine is a brick-dark red, "medium" plus [[carmine]], the crimson pigment made from crushed cochineal insects.

sections.title: Medium plus a cochineal red
sections.body:
The name is a plain modifier on carmine, not an independent coinage [1]. Our library traces it across four older sources: Werner's 1821 nomenclature, Ridgway's 1912 color standards, the ISCC-NBS 1955 lists, and Wikipedia [1]. Werner's 1821 color-naming system, used by naturalists in the field, matched this shade of red to the scarlet ibis, the red oriental poppy, and light red cinnabar [1]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* places a close variant on plate I, hue 3, though that printed plate is itself an aged, approximate scan [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 lists file it in color block 11 [1].

Its books disagree on how distinct it really is: Werner, Ridgway and the ISCC-NBS lists all file a near-duplicate, Scarlet Red, only 1.5 units away [1]. Its nearest named neighbors by measured color are [[vermilion-red]] and [[sweet-brown]], both almost the same hue [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match in 425 of 23,781 paintings, 1.79 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 441 [2]. That makes it more common than 81 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, found in 62 of the 945 paintings we have from that century, 2.8 times the expected rate [2]. Albrecht Dürer is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 6 of his 47 works here [2]. It is most over-represented in paintings from India, at 2.7 times the expected rate, and shares canvases more than chance with Brown Red and Almond [2].
